newsitem.title: BELGIUM: What EU's new treaty may hold.
newsitem.headline: What EU's new treaty may hold.

text.p: European Union leaders meet in the Dutch seaside resort of Noordwijk on Friday for talks on a new EU treaty, due to be agreed at a summit in Amsterdam on June 15 and 16. Here are the main issues at stake:

The draft treaty calls for an "area of freedom and security" to be created by 2002. It is billed as the treaty's centrepiece and designed to attract popular support by guaranteeing a truly border-free Europe. Britain and Ireland are expected to win an opt-out from having to lift their frontiers.
Both concepts, again designed to appeal to citizens, are likely to be incorporated into the treaty in a way that raises them higher on the EU agenda.

Germany and Britain had been holding out against the idea of an employment chapter, fearing it would be an invitation to Brussels to interfere in the labour market, but Britain's new government now supports the move.
Criticised for reacting slowly and ineffectively when foreign policy crises erupt, the EU is looking at ways to boost its voice in world diplomacy.
The treaty is likely to create a forward planning unit to coordinate joint foreign policy actions.

France and Germany are leading a drive to incorporate the Western European Union security grouping fully into the EU as something resembling a European arm of NATO. Britain and the bloc's neutrals -- Sweden, Finland, Ireland and to a lesser extent Austria -- are opposed.
Treaty negotiators are trying to streamline the bloc's decision-making procedures in readiness for its expansion into eastern Europe next decade.

With the British government lifting its predecessor's blanket objection to losing its veto, the new treaty is expected to extend majority voting modestly in certain areas, while retaining unanimity as the rule for sensitive policies.

The future size of the executive European Commission remains one of the toughest issues. Small countries refuse to give up their commissioner; Britain, Germany, France, Italy and Spain, which have two each, may trade one for greater voting clout.
A system of double voting, with a country's population taken into consideration, is also being considered.
FLEXIBILITY: A number of countries have called for the concept of flexibility to be enshrined in the treaty, allowing some EU countries to integrate faster than others.
It is most likely to be introduced in the area of shared immigration and visa policy.
